title: Capacity and Margin
scenario: A manufacturer sells Product X for $90 per unit; variable cost is $52 per unit and each unit requires 2 machine hours. Product Y sells for $120 per unit; variable cost is $72 and each unit requires 3 machine hours. Machine hours are the single binding constraint, with unmet demand for both products and no other differential effects.

questions.q: Which product has the higher contribution margin per unit?
questions.explanation: X contributes $38; Y contributes $48 per unit.

questions.q: Which product has the higher contribution margin per machine hour?

choices.C: Both have the same contribution per machine hour
choices.D: Prioritize solely by contribution per unit, regardless of machine time

questions.explanation: X: $38/2=$19 per hour; Y: $48/3=$16 per hour.

title: Project Evaluation
scenario: A company is evaluating a project requiring $200,000 initially. Expected annual after-tax cash inflows are $80,000 for three years. Required return is 10%. Ignore salvage value. For fractional simple payback, assume the annual cash inflows are received uniformly within each year.

questions.q: Ignoring discounting, what is simple payback?
Why is NPV preferred over simple payback for value-creation decisions?

choices.A: NPV excludes cash flows after the payback date
choices.B: NPV measures accounting income rather than cash flows
choices.D: NPV considers the time value of money and all modeled project cash flows

questions.explanation: NPV discounts all relevant project cash flows at an appropriate required return. Simple payback neither discounts cash flows nor measures benefits received after recovery of the initial investment.

title: Flexible Budget Review
scenario: A service company prepared a monthly static budget for 10,000 service hours. Budgeted variable operating costs are $18 per hour and budgeted fixed operating costs are $90,000. Actual activity was 12,000 hours and actual operating costs were $315,000.

questions.q: What is the flexible-budget operating cost for 12,000 hours?
Compared with the flexible budget, actual operating costs produced what variance?
questions.explanation: Actual $315,000 minus flexible budget $306,000 equals a $9,000 unfavorable variance.

title: Special Order Decision
scenario: A company has unused production capacity. A customer offers to buy 4,000 units for $42 each. Variable manufacturing cost is $27 per unit, and the special order would add $3 per unit of shipping cost. No fixed costs would change, and accepting the order would not reduce normal sales.

questions.q: What is the incremental contribution per special-order unit?
questions.explanation: Incremental revenue $42 less variable manufacturing $27 and shipping $3 equals $12 per unit.

questions.q: What is the total incremental operating income from accepting the order?
questions.explanation: $12 incremental contribution × 4,000 units = $48,000.

title: Flexible budget vs. static budget
scenario: A manufacturer budgeted 10,000 units but produced and sold 9,000. Static cost budget $500,000: $30 variable cost per unit plus $200,000 fixed. Actual total manufacturing cost was $460,000.

questions.q: What is the flexible cost budget at actual volume?
What is the flexible-budget cost variance?
questions.explanation: $470,000 flexible cost less $460,000 actual cost = $10,000 favorable.

written_practice.scenario: Your company budgeted 10,000 units but produced and sold 9,000. Actual total manufacturing cost was $460,000 vs. a static budget of $500,000. Your manager says "we came in $40,000 under budget — great job." You have the cost breakdown: budgeted variable cost $30/unit, budgeted fixed cost $200,000; actual variable cost $29/unit, actual fixed cost $199,000.

questions.q: Compute the flexible budget at 9,000 units.
What is the flexible-budget variance, and is it favorable or unfavorable?
The manager claims the company came in $40,000 under budget. What is wrong with that claim?
questions.model_answer: The static comparison takes credit for $30,000 of "savings" that was just lower volume. Comparing actuals at 9,000 units to a budget built for 10,000 mixes the volume effect with real cost control.

questions.q: Was it actually a good performance? Which cost line drove it?
questions.model_answer: Yes, genuinely favorable — but only $10,000, not $40,000. Variable cost control was good ($29 actual vs $30 budgeted); fixed costs were essentially on target ($199,000 vs $200,000).

title: Master Budget and Sales Forecast
scenario: A manufacturer plans to sell 12,000 units next quarter at $50 each. Beginning finished goods inventory is 1,500 units and management wants ending finished goods inventory of 2,000 units. Variable manufacturing cost is $28 per unit; quarterly fixed manufacturing costs are $90,000.

questions.q: What is budgeted production in units?
questions.explanation: Budgeted production = sales 12,000 + desired ending inventory 2,000 − beginning inventory 1,500 = 12,500 units.

questions.q: What is budgeted manufacturing cost for the quarter?
questions.explanation: Variable manufacturing cost is 12,500 units × $28 = $350,000. Add fixed manufacturing costs of $90,000 for $440,000 total.

title: Direct material and labor variances
scenario: Standards: direct material 3 lb per unit at $5/lb; direct labor 2 hours per unit at $20/hour. Actual output 4,000 units; purchased 13,000 lb at $4.80; used 12,500 lb; labor 8,200 hours at $20.50.

questions.q: What is the materials purchase-price variance?
questions.explanation: ($4.80 − $5) × 13,000 lb purchased = $2,600 favorable.

questions.q: What is the materials usage variance?
questions.explanation: (12,500 used − 4,000 × 3 allowed) × $5 = $2,500 unfavorable.

questions.q: What is the labor rate variance?
What is the labor efficiency variance?
questions.explanation: (8,200 − 8,000 allowed hours) × $20 = $4,000 unfavorable.

written_practice.scenario: Standard cost data: DM 3 lbs/unit at $5.00/lb; DL 2 hrs/unit at $20/hr. Actual: produced 4,000 units; purchased 13,000 lbs at $4.80/lb; used 12,500 lbs; worked 8,200 hrs at $20.50/hr.

questions.q: Compute the direct materials price variance (F/U).
questions.model_answer: ($4.80 − $5.00) × 13,000 lbs purchased = $2,600 F. (Price variance uses quantity purchased, not used.)

questions.q: Compute the direct materials quantity variance (F/U).
Compute the direct labor rate variance (F/U).
Compute the direct labor efficiency variance (F/U).
The purchasing manager is proud of the favorable price variance. What should you tell her?
questions.model_answer: Investigate whether cheaper materials contributed to waste or labor inefficiency. The $2,500 unfavorable usage variance offsets all but $100 of the $2,600 favorable price variance, and the data do not prove a causal link.

title: ROI vs. residual income
scenario: Division X has operating income $900,000 and average operating assets $5,000,000. Hurdle rate 12%. A new project costs $1,000,000 and earns annual operating income $150,000.

questions.q: What are the division's current ROI and residual income?
Which decision best aligns with corporate value creation?

choices.A: Reject because project ROI is below current divisional ROI
choices.B: Reject because residual income is negative
choices.C: Accept because project ROI exceeds 12% and adds $30,000 residual income
choices.D: Accept only if project ROI exceeds 18%

questions.explanation: Project ROI is 15% and project RI is $150,000 − 12% × $1,000,000 = $30,000. Accepting increases value.

written_practice.scenario: Division X has operating income of $900,000 on average operating assets of $5,000,000. The corporate hurdle rate is 12%. A project needs $1,000,000 investment and promises $150,000 annual operating income.

questions.q: Compute the division's current ROI and residual income.
Compute the project's ROI and residual income.
Will the manager accept the project if evaluated on ROI? On residual income?
questions.model_answer: On ROI: reject — 15% drags the 18% average down. On RI: accept — $30,000 > 0 adds to residual income.

questions.q: Which measure produces the better decision for the company, and why?
questions.model_answer: Residual income. The project earns 15%, above the 12% cost of capital, so it creates shareholder value. ROI evaluation causes suboptimization — the manager rejects a value-creating project to protect her percentage. This is the goal-congruence argument for RI/EVA over ROI.

title: Traditional costing vs. ABC
scenario: Total overhead $900,000 allocated traditionally over 50,000 direct labor hours: Product H uses 40,000, L uses 10,000. ABC pools: setups $300,000 (H 20, L 130); machining $400,000 (H 35,000 hours, L 5,000); engineering $200,000 (H 100 hours, L 900).

questions.q: How much traditional overhead is assigned to Product H?
How much ABC overhead is assigned to Product H?
questions.explanation: Setups $40,000 + machining $350,000 + engineering $20,000 = $410,000.

written_practice.scenario: A plant makes two products. Traditional costing applies $900,000 of overhead on direct labor hours: Product H (high-volume, simple): 40,000 DLH; Product L (low-volume, complex): 10,000 DLH. An ABC study finds three pools: setups $300,000 (H: 20 setups, L: 130), machining $400,000 (H: 35,000 hrs, L: 5,000), engineering $200,000 (H: 100 hrs, L: 900).

questions.q: Compute the traditional overhead rate and the overhead assigned to each product.
Compute the ABC activity rates and the overhead assigned to each product.
Which product was overcosted under traditional costing, by how much, and why does this pattern occur?
questions.model_answer: H was overcosted by $310,000 ($720,000 vs $410,000); L was undercosted by the same amount. The pattern: traditional costing spreads batch- and product-level costs by volume, so the high-volume simple product subsidizes the low-volume complex product that actually consumes setups and engineering.

title: Joint costs and further processing
scenario: Joint cost $240,000 produces X (8,000 units at $25 split-off price) and Y (4,000 units at $30 split-off price, or $45 after further processing at $8/unit).

questions.q: Using sales value at split-off, how much joint cost is allocated to X?
What is the incremental profit from further processing Y?
questions.explanation: 4,000 × ($45 − $30 − $8) = $28,000. Joint costs are irrelevant to this decision.

written_practice.scenario: Joint cost of $240,000 produces X (8,000 units, sells at split-off for $25/unit) and Y (4,000 units, sells at split-off for $30/unit, or $45/unit if processed further at $8/unit separable cost).

questions.q: Allocate the joint cost using the sales value at split-off method.
Should Y be processed further? Show the incremental analysis.
questions.model_answer: Incremental revenue = 4,000 × ($45 − $30) = $60,000. Separable cost = 4,000 × $8 = $32,000. Incremental profit = $28,000 → process further.

questions.q: Why are joint costs excluded from the part (b) decision?
questions.model_answer: Joint costs are sunk — they are incurred whether or not Y is processed further. Only the $60,000 incremental revenue and $32,000 separable cost change with the decision. Including allocated joint cost is the classic sunk-cost error.

title: US GAAP to IFRS conversion
scenario: A US manufacturer is converting to IFRS. Its inventory uses LIFO with a $2 million LIFO reserve; a $3 million inventory write-down has recovered $1 million; $5 million development costs meet IFRS capitalization criteria.

questions.q: Which inventory method is prohibited under IFRS?
questions.explanation: IFRS prohibits LIFO. The LIFO reserve indicates the adjustment between LIFO and a non-LIFO basis, subject to conversion specifics.

questions.q: What is the permitted IFRS treatment of a qualifying inventory write-down recovery?

choices.B: Reverse the recovered amount up to the original write-down
choices.C: Recognize the recovery only upon sale

questions.explanation: IAS 2 allows reversal when the reasons for a prior write-down no longer exist, limited to the original write-down.

written_practice.scenario: A US manufacturer is converting its reporting to IFRS for a European parent. The conversion review covers these items (ignore taxes): (1) LIFO inventory with a $2M LIFO reserve; (2) a $3M inventory write-down taken two years ago, of which $1M of value has since recovered; (3) $5M of development costs expensed this year that meet IFRS capitalization criteria; (4) a lawsuit the company judged "reasonably possible" but not "probable."

questions.q: Item 1: what is the IFRS treatment and adjustment direction?
questions.model_answer: LIFO is prohibited under IFRS — restate to FIFO or weighted average. The $2M LIFO reserve is added back to inventory and equity.

questions.q: Item 2: what is the IFRS treatment and adjustment direction?
questions.model_answer: IFRS permits reversal of inventory write-downs: restore the recovered $1M through profit (capped at the original write-down).

questions.q: Item 3: what is the IFRS treatment and adjustment direction?
questions.model_answer: Capitalize the $5M as an intangible asset (amortized over useful life) instead of expensing; equity rises by the unamortized amount.

questions.q: Item 4: what changes under IFRS, if anything?
questions.model_answer: IFRS accrues contingencies at "more likely than not" — a "reasonably possible" item that GAAP leaves unaccrued may still clear the IFRS bar; if so, accrue the estimable amount, reducing equity.

questions.q: Which adjustments increase IFRS equity relative to GAAP, and why?
questions.model_answer: Items 1–3 increase equity (inventory and asset recognition); item 4 may decrease it. Net effect: IFRS equity is typically higher for this profile, driven by LIFO elimination and development capitalization.

title: ASC 606 allocation
scenario: Software contract price $1.2 million, including a distinct license delivered at signing and distinct implementation services over six months. Standalone prices: license $1,000,000; services $250,000. Cash received at signing.

questions.q: What transaction price is allocated to the license?
questions.explanation: $1.2 million × ($1 million/$1.25 million) = $960,000, assuming the distinct license transfers at signing.

questions.q: How much service revenue is recognized per month over six months?
questions.explanation: Allocated services price $240,000 / 6 months = $40,000 monthly.

written_practice.scenario: A software company signs a $1.2M contract: $900,000 license (delivered at signing) and $300,000 of implementation services (delivered evenly over 6 months). The standalone prices are $1,000,000 and $250,000. Cash is received in full at signing. Assume the license and implementation are distinct obligations and control of the license transfers at signing.

questions.q: How many performance obligations are there, and what are they?
questions.model_answer: Two: the license and the implementation services — each is distinct (the customer can benefit from each separately).

questions.q: How is the $1.2M transaction price allocated?
How much revenue is recognized at signing, and per month thereafter?
questions.model_answer: At signing: $960,000 (license delivered). Monthly: $240,000 ÷ 6 = $40,000 as services are performed.

questions.q: What is recorded at signing for the cash received in excess of revenue recognized?
questions.model_answer: Cash $1.2M vs revenue $960,000 → a $240,000 contract liability (deferred revenue), drawn down as services are performed. Control transferred — not cash receipt — drives recognition.

title: Control deficiencies at a manufacturer
scenario: A 40-person manufacturer has one bookkeeper who signs checks under $5,000, posts to the ledger, and reconciles the bank. Warehouse staff count inventory without independent recount. Purchases below $5,000 receive no review.

questions.q: Which is the clearest segregation-of-duties deficiency?

choices.B: Bookkeeper signs checks, records transactions, and reconciles bank

questions.explanation: Combining cash authorization/custody, recordkeeping, and reconciliation undermines independent control.

questions.q: Which improvement best addresses cash disbursement risk?

choices.A: Have the bookkeeper also approve all vendors
choices.D: Have an independent person review reconciliations and approve disbursements

questions.explanation: Independent review and authorization compensate for limited staffing and separate incompatible duties.

written_practice.scenario: A 40-employee manufacturer has: the owner approves all purchases over $5,000 but never reviews anything under that; the bookkeeper writes checks, signs them (under $5,000), reconciles the bank account, and posts to the ledger; inventory counts are done annually by the warehouse staff with no independent recount; there is no audit committee and no internal audit function.

questions.q: Name three control deficiencies and the COSO component each one hits.
questions.model_answer: Any three: (1) Bookkeeper holds authorization (signing), custody (checks), and recordkeeping (ledger, reconciliation) — segregation-of-duties failure under control activities. (2) Purchases under $5,000 have no review — authorization gap under control activities. (3) Inventory counts lack independence — control activities. (4) No audit committee or internal audit — governance/monitoring gap under control environment and monitoring activities.

questions.q: Which deficiency is most severe, and could it constitute a material weakness? Why or why not?
questions.model_answer: The bookkeeper's combined duties are most severe: custody + recordkeeping + authorization over cash disbursements creates the opportunity for disbursement fraud with a reasonable possibility of material misstatement going undetected — that meets the material weakness definition if disbursement volume is material.

questions.q: Recommend three practical improvements given the company's size.
questions.model_answer: Practical fixes: the owner (or a second person) signs all checks and reviews the bank reconciliation; the bookkeeper posts but doesn't reconcile; independent spot-counts of inventory; the owner reviews a monthly disbursement listing as a compensating control.

title: Cash-receipts controls
scenario: A 200-employee company with a centralized accounting department wants stronger controls over incoming payments and receivables.

questions.q: Which is primarily a detective cash-receipts control?
questions.explanation: Independent reconciliation identifies errors or irregularities after processing; the other choices are preventive.

questions.q: Which duties should be separated?

choices.A: Cash custody and recordkeeping can always be combined
choices.C: Cash custody, accounts receivable posting, and bank reconciliation
choices.D: No separation is needed if an ERP is installed

questions.explanation: Separating custody, recording, and reconciliation reduces opportunity to conceal diversion of receipts.

written_practice.scenario: A 200-employee company with a centralized accounting department needs key controls over cash receipts.

questions.q: Give two preventive controls.
questions.model_answer: Any two: segregation of duties; lockbox or electronic payments to reduce cash handling; restrictive endorsement of checks immediately on receipt; pre-numbered receipts.

questions.q: Give two detective controls.
questions.model_answer: Any two: daily reconciliation of cash to receipts; bank reconciliation by someone independent of the receipts function; surprise cash counts; exception reports on discounts and voids.

questions.q: Give one corrective control.
questions.model_answer: Fidelity bond/insurance recovery procedures; documented incident response and reconstruction of accounts from backup records.

questions.q: What segregation of duties is required?
questions.model_answer: Separate opening mail/logging receipts, custody of cash, recording in AR, and reconciling — no one person spans custody and recordkeeping; the bank reconciliation sits outside the receipts function.

questions.q: How does the fraud triangle explain why these controls matter?
questions.model_answer: Pressure and rationalization live in people's heads — the company can't control them. Opportunity is the controllable leg: segregation, reconciliations, and surprise counts shrink opportunity, and visible controls also strengthen the control environment, making rationalization harder.

title: ERP selection and implementation
scenario: A distributor is replacing disconnected accounting, inventory, and sales systems with an ERP. Implementation quotes range from $800,000 to $1.5 million over 18 months.

questions.q: Which implementation approach reduces disruption by rolling out one module or site first?
questions.explanation: Phased rollout allows stabilization and learning before broader deployment, though the right approach depends on dependencies.

questions.q: What should the controller own during ERP implementation?

choices.D: Financial requirements, embedded controls, data quality, and user acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Finance owns the control and data-quality outcomes, not necessarily the software code.

written_practice.scenario: A mid-size distributor is selecting an ERP to replace disconnected accounting, inventory, and sales systems. Implementation quotes range from $800,000 to $1.5M over 18 months.

questions.q: What are the three most important benefits of the ERP for this company?
questions.model_answer: A single central database — inventory, sales, and accounting finally agree; process integration across order-to-cash; real-time visibility with built-in controls and audit trails.

questions.q: What are the three biggest risks of the implementation?
questions.model_answer: Cost and timeline overruns; business disruption during cutover (orders can't ship); rigidity — processes must conform to the software, and a bad fit cripples operations.

questions.q: Recommend a conversion approach and justify it.
questions.model_answer: Use a phased or pilot conversion: convert one module or site first, stabilize, then roll out. Parallel operation can reduce cutover risk but requires duplicate work for the overlap period. Direct cutover creates more immediate disruption risk.

questions.q: What role should the controller play in the project?
questions.model_answer: Define requirements, design controls into the workflows (approvals, segregation, edit checks), lead user-acceptance testing, and run the post-implementation review. Not coding — owning control and data-quality outcomes.

title: Building analytics maturity
scenario: A retail chain has monthly descriptive sales reports and wants to reduce stockouts and markdowns through more advanced analytics.

questions.q: Which analytics type recommends reorder quantities to optimize costs?
questions.explanation: Prescriptive analytics recommends decisions or actions subject to objectives and constraints.

questions.q: Which analytics type forecasts SKU-store demand using history and seasonality?
questions.explanation: Predictive analytics forecasts likely future outcomes.

written_practice.scenario: A retail chain has basic monthly sales reports (descriptive) and wants to build analytics maturity to reduce stockouts and markdowns.

questions.q: Describe what diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics would each look like for this goal.
questions.model_answer: Diagnostic: drill into stockout patterns — which SKUs, stores, days of week; correlate with promotions and lead times. Predictive: forecast demand by SKU-store using history, seasonality, and promotions. Prescriptive: optimization recommending reorder quantities and timing to minimize the combined stockout, holding, and markdown cost.

questions.q: What data governance and quality foundations must be in place first?
questions.model_answer: Governance first: consistent SKU/store definitions across systems; complete and timely sales and inventory feeds; accurate POS data. Models built on dirty data produce confident wrong answers.

questions.q: Where could RPA help, and where would it be the wrong tool?
questions.model_answer: RPA fits rule-based, repetitive, structured work: pulling daily reports, loading POS feeds, reconciling inventory counts. Wrong tool for demand forecasting itself (needs ML, not fixed rules) and for deciding markdown strategy (judgment under uncertainty).

title: Special order with idle capacity
scenario: A manufacturer is considering a special order for 2,000 units at $38/unit. Normal price is $55, unit variable cost is $32, and the plant has idle capacity. Fixed costs are $400,000 and won't change.

written_practice.scenario: A manufacturer is considering a special order for 2,000 units at $38/unit. Normal price is $55, unit variable cost is $32, and the plant has idle capacity. Fixed costs are $400,000 and won't change.

questions.q: Show the incremental analysis. Should the order be accepted on financial grounds?
questions.model_answer: Incremental contribution margin = ($38 − $32) × 2,000 = $12,000 positive → accept. Fixed costs are irrelevant — they don't change.

questions.q: Name two qualitative factors management should weigh.
questions.model_answer: Any two: Will regular customers find out and demand the lower price? Does it damage brand positioning? Is this a one-time order or the start of a long-term low-margin customer? Will it eat capacity needed for future full-price orders?

questions.q: How does your answer change if the plant is operating at full capacity?
questions.model_answer: At full capacity, accepting displaces regular sales — the relevant cost becomes the forgone regular contribution margin of $55 − $32 = $23/unit, which exceeds the $6/unit gained on the special order → reject, unless strategic reasons dominate.
